claims.text: As-fabricated additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components may contain fabrication-induced defects.
The proposed intervention is joint optimization of laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate.
Laser power and scanning speed affect the processability of laser-processed high-entropy alloys.
Powder feed rate is an applicable optimization variable during laser powder bed fusion.
Optimizing the stated process parameters can improve the dimensional precision of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Optimizing the stated process parameters can improve the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Optimizing processing conditions can reduce fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Changes in laser-processing parameters influence the resulting microstructure.
Changes in laser-processing parameters influence defect formation and part density.
The altered microstructure and defect population cause improved dimensional precision.
The altered microstructure and defect population cause improved mechanical integrity.
The current fabrication baseline produces defects and lacks dimensional precision.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to laser powder bed fusion under relevant temperature, atmosphere, and post-processing conditions.
Equipment capabilities and material properties limit the achievable benefit from process optimization.
Optimal process parameters and their effects may differ among high-entropy alloys and operating conditions.
Optimized and non-optimized parameter sets will be compared using dimensional precision, mechanical integrity, and defect measurements.
Failure to improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity, or failure to reduce defects, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention includes powder feed rate, but the stated process is laser powder bed fusion; the cited powder-feed evidence concerns laser cladding rather than powder bed fusion.
